clue.text: This country air refreshes, as even he quoted, with golf

indicators.note: to refresh something is to make it over anew, so these letters are given a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written
G is golf in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A patriotic boast that the nation's fresh air is as bracing as a famous golfer once said.
explanation.walkthrough: 'This country air' looks like talk of fresh breezes, but air means a tune. The fourteen letters of AS EVEN HE QUOTED plus G are rearranged into the four-word answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The national anthem of the United Kingdom is the song, or air, of this country.

clue.text: What experts are said to know about religious beliefs

indicators.note: the vegetable word goes about, or around, the word for religious

parts.words: What experts are said to know
parts.note: experts are said to know their onions, a British idiom for being knowledgeable
pi is informal British for pious or religious

explanation.surface: Experts are reputed to understand religious beliefs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'To know your onions' is a British idiom for knowing your subject well; pi (short for pious) is old school slang.
explanation.definitionFit: Views or convictions a person holds are their opinions.

clue.text: Discontented seaman who constantly wants grass?

indicators.note: discontented means the word loses its contents, leaving only its outside

parts.note: the first and last letters of seaman
an itcher is one who itches for things, constantly wanting

explanation.surface: An unhappy sailor who keeps craving grass to smoke.
explanation.walkthrough: Grass seems to be cannabis, but it is British slang for an informer, the person who tells on others.
explanation.definitionFit: An informer who tells tales to the police is a grass or a sneak.

clue.text: Hit one's head in stuck-up pet and tear away from meeting

indicators.note: the head of one goes in the reversed pet word
in a down clue, stuck up means the word is written upwards

parts.note: luv is an informal endearment like pet

indicators.note: head points to the first letter

parts.note: first letter of one

indicators.note: away from means the tearing word is taken off the meeting word

parts.note: a rendezvous is a meeting
rend means tear

explanation.surface: A stuck-up pet bangs its head and runs off from a gathering.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hit' looks like a verb, but it is a chart hit: ABBA's 1979 song. Luv is the northern English endearment; in a down entry 'stuck-up' reads it upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A popular ABBA single, so a chart success, is the answer.

clue.text: Only a very little feast!

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a tiny amount, as in 'not a' followed by the word
second meaning: the Christian festival of Whitsun, Pentecost

explanation.walkthrough: The exclamation mark makes a small feast sound like a complaint about stingy portions; the two halves are separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: Whitsun is the church festival seven weeks after Easter, and a tiny bit is a jot or iota.

clue.text: Well-oiled forelocks, the last as topknot?

indicators.note: the final letter is moved up to sit at the top of the word, as a topknot does

parts.note: quiffs are tufts of hair brushed up over the forehead

explanation.surface: Greased-up hair styled with a final twist into a topknot.
explanation.walkthrough: Well-oiled looks like hair grease, but it means drunk; in a down clue the top is the start, so QUIFFS has its S moved to the front.
explanation.definitionFit: Being well-oiled is slang for tipsy, and this is a British slang word for slightly drunk.

clue.text: As it happens, society newbie's over worry

indicators.note: over tells us to turn the combined letters upside down, reading them upwards in this down entry

parts.note: live broadcast is shown as it happens
a deb (debutante) is a young woman newly entering society

explanation.surface: A debutante is fretting right now about the season.
explanation.walkthrough: A debutante, deb for short, was a young upper-class woman presented at court in her first season.
explanation.definitionFit: To bedevil is to plague or torment, to trouble someone persistently.

clue.text: Performing party engaged by 9 herself

indicators.note: engaged by means held within the word that follows

parts.note: the Queen famously refers to herself as 'one'
a stag is a party for a man about to marry

explanation.surface: The Queen herself was booked for a party.
explanation.walkthrough: 9 is THE QUEEN, whose royal 'one' is the outer piece; STAG sits inside it after its first two letters.
explanation.definitionFit: An actor appearing before an audience is performing in public.

clue.text: See 1
Reasoning, preposterously, man-eating sharks will swim in it?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a fallacious argument in which each premise rests on the conclusion

definitions.text: man-eating sharks will swim in it
definitions.meaning: second meaning, playful: a ring of savage sharks circling their prey

explanation.walkthrough: The phrase names a logical fallacy, and taken literally it pictures the ring that ferocious sharks swim round a victim before they strike.
explanation.definitionFit: Circular argument that keeps proving itself is a classic logical fault, while sharks circling are a literally vicious ring.

clue.text: Dispatched rubbish back through grating

indicators.note: one word placed through another means it goes inside it

parts.note: something dispatched has been sent

indicators.note: back tells us to read the word for rubbish in reverse

parts.note: dirt is rubbish or filth

explanation.surface: Waste that was sent away comes back up through a drain grating.
explanation.walkthrough: 'grating' looks like a drain cover, but it is the adjective for a harsh, jarring noise.
explanation.definitionFit: A strident voice is loud and harsh, just as a grating noise jars on the ear.

clue.text: Very much a bad egg?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the colloquial intensifier, as in 'I miss her' followed by the phrase
second meaning, playful: an egg gone off is literally a putrid thing

explanation.walkthrough: A bad egg is usually a rogue, but here it is simply an egg that has gone off. The phrase is also British slang for 'enormously', as in 'it hurt' followed by it.
explanation.definitionFit: Colloquially the phrase intensifies a verb, meaning a great deal; literally, a spoiled egg is a putrid object.

clue.text: See 10
Draining spirit bottles order provided in past

indicators.note: a word that bottles another holds it inside, as a bottle holds a drink

parts.note: zing is spirit or liveliness
OM is the Order of Merit

indicators.note: the word for provided sits in the word for past

parts.note: by can mean past, as in 'walk by'
if means provided, as a condition

explanation.surface: Someone draining a bottle of spirits orders more, provided they did so before.
explanation.walkthrough: 'spirit' and 'bottles' suggest a drinks cabinet, but spirit is liveliness and bottles is a containment signal; the Order of Merit is a British honour.
explanation.definitionFit: To zombify someone is to sap their life and energy until they move like the walking dead.

clue.text: 24 fell in tour, exemplifying this?

indicators.note: 24 is ROTTEN, and rotten letters are spoiled and must be put back together

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone who falls badly ill on a trip abroad suffers rotten luck.
explanation.walkthrough: 24 refers to ROTTEN, here used as the anagram signal on FELL IN TOUR; falling ill on tour is itself an example of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Falling sick on holiday is a clear case of bad luck or misfortune.

clue.text: A joint rolled furtively by greenkeeper

indicators.note: rolled means the letters are turned over and read the other way
furtively means the letters are tucked out of sight within the word that follows

parts.note: the letters sit inside this word

explanation.surface: A greenkeeper secretly rolls a cannabis joint on the golf course.
explanation.walkthrough: A joint rolled furtively sounds like cannabis; the joint is a body part, and its letters lie backwards in greenKEEPer's middle stretch.
explanation.definitionFit: The knee is the hinge joint of the human leg, between thigh and shin.

clue.text: This Landlord may have free Merlot too!

indicators.note: free here means loosened and set at liberty, so the letters are reworked into a new arrangement

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A pub landlord who gives away Merlot as well!
explanation.walkthrough: The Landlord sounds like a publican pouring free wine, but it is a property owner advertising accommodation.
explanation.definitionFit: A property owner with vacant accommodation advertises it with this sign on the window.

clue.text: Exit left after processing data collection

indicators.note: data processing reworks input, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone leaves the office after processing a pile of data.
explanation.definitionFit: A computer document holding plain characters is a stored collection of data.

clue.text: In doing a turn as before, it's boring me too

indicators.note: in puts the boring word within the other pieces
doing a turn means the little word spins around backwards

parts.note: ere is an old word for before
meh is the shrug of someone finding something dull

explanation.surface: A stage act repeated exactly as before bores the speaker too.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Meh' is a modern interjection of boredom, so 'it's boring' is what someone says with it; 'ere' is the poetic word for before.
explanation.definitionFit: A reply agreeing with someone, saying the same applies to the speaker as well.

clue.text: Inverted hearts and crown containing letter's last words

indicators.note: containing means the letter goes inside the other pieces
in a down clue, inverted means the pieces read upwards

parts.note: H is the card-suit abbreviation for hearts
the pate is the crown of the head
pi is a Greek letter

explanation.surface: A card player's last words on upended hearts and a crown.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down entry 'Inverted' reads the pieces upwards; the pate is the top of the head, its crown.
explanation.definitionFit: An inscription on a gravestone gives the final words commemorating the dead.

clue.text: One noble and virtuous festive occasion enjoyed

parts.note: a gala is a festive celebration
had can mean enjoyed, as in 'had a good time'

explanation.surface: A noble, virtuous figure who enjoyed a festive celebration.
explanation.walkthrough: Galahad was the purest knight of King Arthur's Round Table, who found the Holy Grail.
explanation.definitionFit: The Arthurian knight is a byword for chivalry and purity of character.

clue.text: Questions that will test PM now, presumably

parts.note: by now that morning is presumably a thing of the past, a former one: ex
when it is PM, afternoon, the time before it was AM, morning

explanation.surface: Reporters prepare tough questions to grill the Prime Minister now.
explanation.walkthrough: PM looks like the Prime Minister, but it is post meridiem: once it is afternoon the morning is over, so the time is an EX-AM, a former morning.
explanation.definitionFit: A school or university test consists of a set of written or spoken questions.

clue.text: Episcopalianism sadly has no place for instruction of organists?

indicators.note: sadly signals that the letters are in a sorry, jumbled state and must be reworked

parts.note: the fodder, from which the letters of the word for place are taken
these letters are removed from the fodder

explanation.surface: The Episcopal church sadly has no room left for its organists' instructions.
explanation.walkthrough: Strike P, L, A, C, E from EPISCOPALIANISM and rearrange the remaining ten letters. The question mark warns that organists are only one kind of musician given this direction.
explanation.definitionFit: A score marking telling musicians, organists included, to play very softly.

clue.text: Pre-analytically know about Tuesday being successful

indicators.note: about means the successful phrase wraps around the day

parts.note: 'in it' to win it: in it suggests being in contention, successful

explanation.surface: Someone senses beforehand that Tuesday will go well.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In it' means in contention, with a chance of success, as in 'in it to win it'.
explanation.definitionFit: To grasp something by instinct, without reasoning it out, is to perceive it immediately.

clue.text: See 11
In which we raise a glass to a hustler's crowning moment?

definitions.text: In which we raise a glass

parts.note: a sting is a con artist's elaborate swindle, the climax of a hustler's work

explanation.surface: Drinkers raise their glasses in celebration of a con man's greatest coup.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads like a toast to a hustler; read the answer as TO A STING, a sting being a hustler's big confidence trick.
explanation.definitionFit: Drinking someone's health is done by lifting glasses together in salute.

clue.text: What Dear John letter tells me, any more talent?

parts.words: What Dear John letter tells me
parts.note: a Dear John letter ends a relationship, and its message to me is a refusal: no
the letter means there is no couple, no 'us', any more

explanation.surface: A jilted lover asks if, after a break-up letter, they have any talent left.
explanation.walkthrough: A Dear John letter is a break-up note; its message is 'no us any more'. The question mark flags nous as common sense, a loose sort of talent.
explanation.definitionFit: Nous is practical good sense or know-how, a kind of natural aptitude.

clue.text: Line of underground humour not new in summer month

indicators.note: in places the humour word inside what is left of the month
not tells us to leave out the letter for new

parts.note: June is a summer month in the northern hemisphere
bile is one of the four humours of old medicine

explanation.surface: Underground humour, without anything new, in a summer month.
explanation.walkthrough: This is a London Underground line, built for Elizabeth II's 1977 Silver Jubilee. BILE goes inside JUE (June less N); the four humours were bodily fluids once thought to govern temperament.
explanation.definitionFit: London's Tube network includes a route, coloured grey, opened in 1979 and named for the Queen's anniversary.

clue.text: Boring choice, doing home steely grey

indicators.note: boring means drilling into, so the pieces go inside the word for choice

parts.note: a plum job is a choice one
at can mean doing, as in 'what are you at?'
in means at home

explanation.surface: A dull choice of a steel-grey colour for doing up the home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boring' looks like the adjective for dull, but it is the insertion signal; a plum job is a choice one.
explanation.definitionFit: The precious metal has a silvery grey colour, and its name is used for that shade.

clue.text: One's parting not so easy to endure

definitions.meaning: first meaning: one who parts or cuts things off, a person who severs
second meaning: harsher, the comparative of a word meaning harsh

explanation.walkthrough: 'One's parting' sounds like someone leaving; read it as 'one who is parting' something, a cutter.
explanation.definitionFit: A severer is someone who cuts things apart, and severer is also the comparative meaning harsher or more grievous.
